summary: Registers media types for the ECMAScript and JavaScript programming languages and sets conformance requirements for implementations. It is informational and was later replaced by RFC 9239.

eli5.summary: A label that tells a browser this file contains JavaScript code. This memo gives that label.

questions: what is the javascript mime type
how does browser detect file encoding
subtitle: Standard labels to tell web servers that a file contains JavaScript or ECMAScript code.

tldr.problem: Many different, non-standard labels have been used over the years to mark files as JavaScript or ECMAScript code, leading to interoperability problems and inconsistent handling.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers four standard media types: two obsolete ones (text/javascript and text/ecmascript) and two recommended ones (application/javascript and application/ecmascript), along with rules for character encoding and error handling.
tldr.outcome: Browsers and servers now have a consistent, standardized way to recognize and handle JavaScript code based on its media type label.

today: RFC 4329 was obsoleted by RFC 9239 in August 2022, which updates the media type registrations and clarifies support for modern JavaScript versions.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
A media type is a label that tells a web server, browser or email program what kind of file it is. For example, text/html means HTML, and image/png means a PNG image.

In the early days of the web, people invented many different labels for JavaScript files, such as text/javascript, application/javascript, text/x-javascript, and many others. This document registers the standard media types for JavaScript and ECMAScript, the standardized language that JavaScript is based on. It also defines rules for how these files should be encoded and handled.
sections.eli5: Browsers need a name to recognize JavaScript code. Different people used different names, so files got confused. This document picks the right names that everyone should use.

sections.title: Four Media Types
sections.content:
The RFC registers four media types. Two are marked as obsolete: text/javascript and text/ecmascript. These use the text category, but using text for executable code creates problems, so they are deprecated in favor of the application category.

The two recommended types are application/javascript (for JavaScript code written to the JavaScript 1.5 specification) and application/ecmascript (for code written to the ECMA-262 standard). The application/javascript type is the most widely used today. Both types support an optional charset parameter to specify the character encoding (such as UTF-8).
sections.eli5: There are two good names: application/javascript for JavaScript and application/ecmascript for standard ECMAScript. The old names text/javascript and text/ecmascript still work but should not be used for new files.

sections.title: Character Encoding
sections.content:
JavaScript source code is text that must be encoded using a character encoding scheme, such as UTF-8. The RFC defines how browsers and servers determine which encoding was used.

Implementations MUST support UTF-8. They can also support other encodings. The algorithm checks, in order: (1) a charset parameter in the media type if present, (2) a Unicode byte order mark (a special code at the start of the file), and (3) a default to UTF-8. If binary source text contains invalid bytes for the detected encoding, the implementation MUST treat it as unsupported rather than guessing a different encoding.
sections.eli5: JavaScript is text. The browser needs to know what alphabet (encoding) the text uses. It checks the label, then looks for clues in the file, then assumes UTF-8. It will not guess.

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
Running untrusted JavaScript is dangerous. Any implementation that executes scripts MUST consider the threat of code injection attacks, where an attacker tricks the code into running harmful commands. Implementations MUST protect against denial-of-service attacks that try to freeze the browser by running infinite loops or using too much memory.

Implementations that support dynamically generated code execution (such as the eval function) must be especially careful about where the input comes from. Scripts embedded in HTML documents inherit the security constraints of the HTML document format. The choice of character encoding can also affect security: if the encoding is wrong, bytes that look like safe characters might actually be commands in the correct encoding.
sections.eli5: Running code from the internet is risky. The browser must stop bad code from stealing passwords, crashing the computer, or doing other harm. Wrong encoding can hide dangerous code, so the browser must detect it correctly.
